#250. SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

“Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026.”

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”

The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

#248. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#247. UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy

Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions over migrant crossings.

A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.

Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.

The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.

Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.

After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.

Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.

During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."

He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.

Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.

Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.

The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).

"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.

Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.

He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.

Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.

The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.

Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.

Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.

Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.

The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.

The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."

Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.

Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.

Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.

Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

#246. Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

#244. The US national cyber director is stepping down

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.

In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

#242. “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science

Modern genetics does not support claims of innate racial differences in intelligence.

At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.

How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.

Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.

In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.

Skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.

We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supported today. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.

Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.

While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.

When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.

Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.

The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.

Meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.

What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic—something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.

As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.

Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.

Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.

Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.

Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.

No matter which way you look at these issues—from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology, or psychology—hereditarianism does not hold up.

To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is important to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups—not just race but class—were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.

If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilization laws that aimed to “improve” society by preventing—without their consent—the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.

In the decades after the Second World War, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognized racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.

Yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science said, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a nonprofit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.

The Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century—including supporting Mankind Quarterly—when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channeled its remaining funds into a new company, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.

Given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigor in genetics or biology.

Instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology, has described it as a “community project… with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders, and historiography.”

Behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers, and others in gatekeeping roles, which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.

Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal that has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally published editorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.

There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist toward the end of the 20th century.

Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a “hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicize his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.

Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed new editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.

However, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distasteful.” It claimed—relying on race science’s unscientific arguments—that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.

Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.

The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.

Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.

But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics that have long since been settled.

We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.

Jonathan R. Goodman is Assistant Research Professor, Psychiatry, University of Cambridge, and Rebecca Sear is Director of the Centre for Culture and Evolution, Brunel University of London.

#240. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#239. Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear

Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”

Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people.

According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

#238. Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain

Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.

Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.

Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."

The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.

​Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.

"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.

Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to ​2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.

Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.

Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.

Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."

Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

#236. Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels

Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes

It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.

Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah, whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.

It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play.

(WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.)

Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.)

Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield: Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb.

Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.

The film ends on a suitably bittersweet note, and while Yamazaki hasn’t dropped any hints about a possible third film in the series, we’d love to learn more about Noriko’s strangely symbiotic connection to Godzilla via the G-cells in her bloodstream. Long may he reign.

Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

#235. Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter

Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.

From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.

You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.

The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.

Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work, is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.

The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.

If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).

Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.

The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.

Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

Starting at $479, the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.

Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.

If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.

Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.

The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.

Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.

Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.

The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

#232. A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

“Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”

Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 153, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, thank you for tearing yourself away from GTA to be here, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)

This week, I’ve been reading about nuclear radiation and F1 brains and phone scammers, watching about 10 minutes of Madden before bailing, playing a lot of Madden NFL instead, learning my way around Instagram Edits on the Mac, trying the 12-3-30 workout while watching Mission: Impossible movies in half-hour increments, getting my new Apple HomeView up and running (still don’t know why I bought one…), and dreaming up stuff to do with the Flipper One.

I also have for you the game of the year (decade? century?), a couple of great new productivity tools, a Netflix take on the FTX story, and much more. But mostly, it’s GTA week. Let’s do it.

Also, programming note: Installer is off next week. It’s Thanksgiving, there’s food to eat and football to watch. Hope you have a great couple of weeks, and we’ll be so back in December.

You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.

I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”

I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.

The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.

Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.

Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.

I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!

iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.

One of the most underrated strange things about the tech industry is how much The Social Network changed the way people think about Mark Zuckerberg. Yes, the movie takes huge liberties, and yes, every single person involved with the movie was quick to remind us that it was fiction. But for so many people, Jesse Eisenberg’s character just became who Zuck was.

The new trailer looks fabulous, all the early buzz about the movie seems to be great, and the movie absolutely could not be more perfectly timed. It’s apparently a pretty brutal look at Altman, OpenAI, and the whole AI movement — I wonder how Garfield and his handsomeness might bend the way the world responds. I cannot wait to see this movie.

#229. Three El Salvador soldiers die in explosives accident in Haiti

The soldiers were part of a Salvadoran military contingent deployed to the violence-ridden Caribbean nation last month to rescue four missing airmen. The deployment has widened into an operation against Haiti's gangs.

Three Salvadoran soldiers were killed in Haiti while handling explosives, El Salvador's military said on Friday.

The incident marks the first officially reported deaths since a 2,000-member Salvadoran military contingent was deployed to the gang violence-stricken Caribbean nation last month.

One of the soldiers succumbed to his injuries while being treated in the neighboring Dominican Republic, where he was airlifted to, the El Salvador military said on X.

Another soldier was wounded in the incident and is out of danger, it added.

It was not immediately clear where the blast took place.

The Salvadoran military's statement also did not give any further details on the type of explosives the soldiers were working with.

"We extend our deepest condolences and solidarity to the families of the three deceased," it said.

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent over 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti to rescue four El Salvador airmen — members of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF)—  who went missing after a gang ambush on October 18 in the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince.

The additional troops dispatched by Bukele are not part of the GSF, and the contingent's remit appears to have broadened to stamp out Haitian gangs.

Bukele, who has been known for his tough approach to the gangs in El Salvador, has posted several videos of strikes on residences of gang leaders around Port-au-Prince.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meanwhile, on Friday, Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador to build three new Haitian prisons.

The development follows this week's visit to El Salvador by Haiti's security and justice minister, Patrick Pelissier.

The prisons will be built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, Pelissier said.

Haitian prisons are notoriously overcrowded. In 2024, gang raids in two of the country's biggest penitentiaries saw thousands of inmates being released.

El Salvador, on the other hand, is home to a notorious maximum security mega-prison known as Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).

The country has imprisoned over 90,000 people with no access to family visits ever since entering a state of exception in 2022.

Pelissier visited CECOT during his trip to El Salvador.

"Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again," the Haitian minister said as he praised the mega-prison.

#228. Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B

Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

#227. The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one

The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive

There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a new third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

#226. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.
